proposals.observation: Three GitHub Actions workflows failed on 2026-06-08: "Daily Blog Post" at 08:21, "Weekly Monday Report" at 10:08, and "Funnel-Hack Digest" at 12:49. The content queue shows only 1 post queued against 47 published, meaning the pipeline that feeds new posts has stalled. No commits were recorded in the last 24 hours. The blog is the primary organic entry point for the ICP and a dead pipeline means no new top-of-funnel content is being published.
proposals.proposal: Inspect the daily-blog-post.yml workflow file for the failure root cause. The three consecutive failures across different workflow names on the same day strongly suggest a shared dependency — most likely an expired API key, a changed environment secret name, or a broken import in a shared JS/Python helper the workflows all call. Check the Actions logs for the earliest failure (08:21) first, because the later two likely cascaded from the same cause. Fix the root cause in that file, confirm the secret names in the repo Settings match what the workflow references, and re-run. Do not touch .github/workflows/* files listed in blocked_paths beyond the single failing workflow unless the root cause demands it.

proposals.impact: removes email gate that caused 100% drop-off
proposals.observation: The quiz recorded 1 session, 1 start, and 0 completions in the 48-hour window. The furthest-step distribution shows the single visitor stopped at "email_shown" — meaning the email capture gate is placed before the quiz delivers any value. The visitor arrived from Instagram, started the quiz, hit the email wall, and left. A 0% completion rate from the one measurable session is a clean signal that the gate position is the friction point, not the quiz content itself.
proposals.proposal:
Move the email capture step from before the quiz results to after them. The visitor has already answered questions and invested attention; the results page is the moment of highest perceived value and therefore the correct place to ask for an email. The change is a single reorder of the email-gate component within the Quiz component file. The ask should be framed as: "Get a short written summary of your results sent to your inbox" rather than any urgency-based prompt. This mirrors standard quiz-funnel evidence that gated-after-results completion rates run 20 to 40 percentage points higher than gated-before.

The new email prompt copy should read:

"Want a plain-English version of this sent to your inbox? I write a short note to go with each result type — no sequence, just one email. Drop your address below."

That copy is specific enough to pass the Sultanic test: it names the format (plain-English), the quantity (one email), and removes the fear of being added to a long sequence, which is the real objection a 28-year-old who has signed up to too many funnels already carries into this moment.

proposals.impact: capitalises on 66.67% open rate with a direct coaching CTA
proposals.observation: The Money Vigilance automation has a 66.67% open rate across 12 sends — the strongest open rate of the three active automations by a clear margin. The Money Avoidance sequence sits at 52.63% and Money Worship at 37.5%. A sequence that holds two-thirds of its readers past the subject line is demonstrating real trust and readiness. If the current Money Vigilance sequence ends without a direct offer or a prompt to book a call, that trust is being left sitting idle.
proposals.proposal:
Add a closing email to the Money Vigilance automation that makes a single, direct invitation to book a discovery call with Joel. This email should be the last message in the sequence and should not sell the methodology — the reader already opened every prior email, so the work is to name what comes next, not to re-pitch the premise. The email should be short: four to six sentences, grounded in what a Money Vigilance reader specifically experiences (watching every outgoing pound, feeling safe only when the number is growing, struggling to spend on themselves even when the spending is reasonable), and ending with one link.

The email body should read:

Subject: One thing I notice in people who track everything

If you've got this far in this series, there's a reasonable chance you check your balance more than once a day. Not because you're worried. Because the number going up is the thing that feels safe.

That works, up to a point. The point it stops working is usually quiet — not a crisis, just a slow realisation that you've been careful for years and you're still not sure it's enough.

If that's where you are, a conversation might be worth forty minutes of your time. No prep needed. Just an honest look at what's actually there.

[Book a call — link]

Joel
MSc Behavioural Economics | Qualified Financial Planner
